analysis.one_liner: Makes price gouging during emergencies illegal, with federal and state penalties for large companies.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 20 Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat without any committee action since its referral in July 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for any company to sell a good or service at a "grossly excessive price," at any point in the supply chain. During an emergency like a natural disaster or public health crisis, companies with big revenue or dominant market share would be presumed to be gouging if they raise prices well above their prior or competitors' levels, and could face penalties of up to 5% of their parent company's revenue. Large public companies would also have to disclose their margins and pricing strategies to the SEC after a market shock, and the FTC would get $1 billion to enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially during emergencies when prices spike — hurricane evacuees, households facing utility or grocery price surges after a disaster, and anyone hit by sudden inflation after a supply disruption. State attorneys general also gain a new federal tool to sue on behalf of their residents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers hit by emergency price spikes

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any seller, anywhere in the supply chain, to charge a grossly excessive price, closing the gap left by patchwork state price-gouging laws that only cover declared emergencies.

During an exceptional market shock, large companies (over $1 billion in US revenue) or dominant ones (40%+ seller share or 30%+ buyer share) are presumed to be gouging if they sell above their pre-shock price or competitors' prices, and must prove otherwise with clear and convincing evidence.

Lets the FTC sue in federal court for injunctions, civil penalties up to 5% of a violator's parent company's revenue, and restitution or damages for aggrieved consumers — authority the FTC currently lacks for this kind of conduct.

Empowers every state attorney general to bring the same actions in federal court on behalf of their residents, and requires big public companies to disclose in SEC filings how much of a price increase came from cost changes versus margin expansion.
Appropriates $1 billion to the FTC, available through 2033, to fund the enforcement and rulemaking work.

analysis.who_pays: Large companies — any whose ultimate parent earned over $100 million in US revenue — face penalties of up to 5% of parent revenue per violation, and SEC-registered firms face new quarterly disclosure work after market shocks. Taxpayers fund the $1 billion FTC appropriation. Smaller businesses are exempt if they can show their price increase just reflects their own cost increases.

drawbacks.text: The core standard — a 'grossly excessive price' — is deliberately left for FTC rulemaking to define, with the bill suggesting the agency consider anything at or above 120% of the prior six-month market average; businesses argue that a bright-line cap like that ignores real cost swings and could deter sellers from bringing in scarce supplies during a crisis, when higher prices are partly what draws in more supply.

The affirmative defense for passing on cost increases is only available to companies whose ultimate parent earned under $100 million, so even a large firm whose price rise genuinely tracks outside costs must defend itself with clear and convincing evidence during a shock — a heavier compliance and litigation burden.

The SEC disclosure mandate requires detailed tables of margins, cost changes, and a narrative explaining pricing strategy in filings after any quarter with a market shock, a significant new reporting obligation for issuers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is real: emergency price gouging is widely resented, state laws are inconsistent, and the bill gives both federal and state enforcers teeth with penalties scaled to company size. The strongest objection is design, not principle — a near-automatic cap at roughly 120% of prior prices during shocks, with the burden of proof shifted onto companies, could suppress the price signals that bring supplies into a disaster zone, and the rulemaking needed to calibrate the standard is substantial. On balance the bill targets a specific, well-documented harm, but its breadth is a legitimate concern.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2025 and referred to two House committees, which have taken no action on it so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the Price Gouging Prevention Act of 2025 on July 17, 2025, joined by 12 original cosponsors including Reps. Jayapal, Khanna, Tlaib, DeLauro, and Craig.
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and to the Financial Services Committee, a dual referral that requires both committees to act before the bill can move.
Since the referral, no hearings, markups, votes, or further actions have been recorded on the bill, and all 20 cosponsors are Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet, because nothing has happened: the bill is sitting in committee. If it stays there, the outcome preserves the status quo, in which emergency price spikes face only uneven state-level rules and large sellers face no federal penalty.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; status quo continues

industries.industry: Large retailers, grocery chains, and consumer goods companies
industries.note: Any seller whose ultimate parent earned over $100 million in US revenue could face penalties of up to 5% of parent revenue for grossly excessive prices, at any point in the supply chain. During emergencies, big or dominant sellers would be presumed to be gouging and must prove their price increases just reflect outside costs.

After any quarter with an exceptional market shock, covered issuers must file detailed tables and narratives on price changes, margins, and pricing strategy in their 10-Qs and 10-Ks. This raises compliance costs but also gives investors and enforcers visibility into whether price hikes were driven by costs or by margin expansion.
The bill gives the FTC new authority to sue over price gouging, obtain restitution for consumers, and write the rules defining violations, backed by a $1 billion appropriation available through 2033.
State AGs gain a federal cause of action they can bring in federal or state court to win penalties and restitution for their residents, without preempting state law.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with two committees, has no Republican cosponsors, and no recorded committee action, so the likely path is that it stalls there and dies at the end of the 119th Congress unless House leadership chooses to schedule it. A near-identical version is the kind of consumer-protection bill that majority parties rarely bring up without bipartisan backing.
